extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and patent examiners (Korean Patent Office / Korea)
extracted.subtask_description: Examination guidance and criteria for patent applications in biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics (and procedural rules for collective examination) as applied by the Korean Patent Office; covers disclosure/claim requirements, utility, unity, novelty, inventive step, and procedural requirements for collective examination and expedited processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for collective examination — required forms and attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner requesting collective examination must fill out the request form of collective examination via the Patent-Ro website and attach the 'Notification of to attach additional certified documents stated in request for collective examination'. Documents proving that applications are being practiced or in preparation for practicing may be submitted by showing them to the examiner in charge during the presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: fill out request form via website Patent-Ro and attach specified certified documents; proof-of-practice documents may be shown to examiner during presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of presentation, start, and finishing dates for collective examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner must designate a desired candidate date for presentation (7–14 days after request), a desired start date for collective examination (at least 14 days after presentation), and a desired finishing date within one year after three months from the desired start date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dates must fall in the specified windows; petitioner proposes candidate dates and later the office selects and notifies final dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary examination option with collective examination
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may request preliminary examination when filing for collective examination; if requested, the preliminary examination proceeds according to the preliminary examination interview and post-interview procedures (see chapter 4 references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary examination must be requested at filing for collective examination to be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal and amendment limits after requesting collective examination
rubrics_metrics.description: After the request, some applications among those requested may be withdrawn, but it is not allowed to change or add applications to the collective-examination request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial withdrawal allowed; modification or addition of applications to the request is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality examination for collective examination — eligibility and procedural compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The official in charge must confirm whether applications are eligible for collective examination and whether the request itself satisfies procedural requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a gatekeeping formality check before proceeding to presentation and examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to amend defective collective-examination request (6-day rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the request does not satisfy requirements, the official in charge must notify the petitioner to amend the request form within 6 days from the date of the request; failure to amend within the period may cause the request not to be permitted or the unamended application to be excluded from examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict 6-day amendment window; explicit notice of consequences must be given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and notification of presentation holding date by consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: The official in charge must select the holding date of the collective examination presentation in consultation with the petitioner and the examiner in charge based on proposed candidate dates, then notify the petitioner and examiner in charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dates are finalized by consultation among official, petitioner, and examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation content requirement — explain relation to one product
rubrics_metrics.description: At the collective examination presentation the petitioner must explain the applications and explain that the applications are related to one product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation is in-person to the examiner in charge and must link the applications to a single product to justify collective treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of eligibility for collective examination at presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Official in charge and examiner in charge must consult during presentation to determine whether the applications satisfy requirements for collective examination and which applications are eligible; they also determine start/finish dates in consultation with the petitioner and notify the petitioner of matters determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective-exam eligibility is decided collaboratively at presentation; start/finish dates set accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited-examination requirement when expected start date precedes desired start date (patent/utility model)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the expected start date for an application (patent/utility model) is more than 3 months earlier than the desired start date for other applications in the collective order of receipt, the official in charge can require applicants to file for expedited examination for those applications within a period designated by the official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office may require expedited filing to align examination timing; failure to file expedited examination as required may lead to exclusion from collective examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited-examination requirement for trademark/design in collective examination (1-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the expected start date for trademark/design applications is more than a month earlier than the desired start date of the collective examination, the official in charge may require applicants to file for expedited examination within a period designated by the official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark/design threshold is 1 month; similar consequences for non-compliance as with patents/utility models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion for failure to request expedited examination or for certain trademark applications
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant does not file the requested expedited examination within the period, or if the expedited-examination request is for a trademark application that is excluded from 'practicing or preparation for practicing', the application is deemed excluded from the collective examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office may exclude non-compliant or ineligible applications from collective treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documents acceptable to prove practicing or preparation for practicing (expedited exam evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: To support expedited examination based on practicing or preparation for practicing, acceptable documents include: (i) full-size photograph of test product, sample, catalog with photograph, etc.; (ii) investment records from VC or new-technology project investment cooperatives; (iii) loan records from financial institutions; (iv) contracts about practice of application technology; (v) other documents proving preparation of practicing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated list of evidential documents that may substantiate practicing/preparation for practicing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of submission by examiner reading of evidential documents
rubrics_metrics.description: If evidential documents are submitted for expedited examination, submission may be substituted by the examiner reading the documents; when the examiner reads such documents, the examiner should state the reading date, place, and contents on the examination report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must formally record reading of substituted evidential documents (date/place/contents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeding with collective examination — start/finish and handling documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner in charge should start the collective examination on the expected start date and should finish dealing with any documents submitted during the examination until the expected finishing date; exceptions allowed for inevitable reasons such as additional prior-art searching or discovery of new grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners aim to adhere to the scheduled examination window but may extend for justified reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirement — specific, substantial, credible utility for genes/proteins
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions of a gene or a protein encoded by the gene, the description must state a specific, substantial and credible utility in the description of the invention; without such assertion or inference, the invention is not considered industrially applicable under Article 29(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere discovery of a gene/protein without a clear utility is insufficient; utility must be concrete and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and well-established utility requirement for chemical-substance/biotech inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: For chemical substances (including genes) the description requirements involve a well-established utility and enablement: a person skilled in the art must be able to make and use the claimed invention as of the filing date, and the utility should be clearly and sufficiently stated since the claimed substance cannot be used without clear description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions cited (e.g., 2007HEO5116) support strict enablement and utility; mere discovery of existence of a natural product generally insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim content for genes and DNA fragments — sequence specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: A gene and a DNA fragment should be described by specifying the sequence thereof. Use of expressions like 'a sequence having ~% homology with a specific reference sequence' in the claim is not permitted in principle unless the description provides solid evidence that variants with that homology contain the same activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be sequence-specific; broad homology-based claim language rarely accepted without supporting description and evidence (case law referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming structural genes by amino acid sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: A structural gene may be described in a claim by specifying the amino acid sequence of the protein encoded by the gene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protein amino-acid sequence can serve to define the corresponding gene in claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic variants — disclosure of position and content
rubrics_metrics.description: When expressions such as 'deletion', 'substitution' or 'addition' are used in relation to a sequence, the position and the content of those variants should be specifically disclosed. If specific examples of genetic variants are provided, it may be permitted to define claims by limiting function and scope of variants, but merely describing hybridization conditions is insufficient to specify scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High specificity required for variant claims; functional-limited variant claims permitted only with concrete supporting examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protein and recombinant protein claim description
rubrics_metrics.description: A protein and a recombinant protein should be described by specifying the amino acid sequence or the nucleic acid sequence of the structural gene encoding the protein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence-based description is the norm for protein-related claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protein variants — position/content disclosure and exceptional function-based claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming protein variants using terms like 'deletion', 'substitution', 'addition', the position and content must be clearly described. Under exceptional circumstances, if there are specific and sufficient examples of a protein variant in the description, it is permitted to describe the invention by limiting the function of the protein and the scope of the variant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function-based variant claims allowed only as exceptions supported by concrete exemplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: When protein sequence cannot be specified — alternate claim descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: If a protein cannot be specified by its amino-acid sequence, it may be described in the claim by limiting all of functions, physicochemical properties, origin/source, and method for producing the protein; in this case there must be reasonable grounds for why the protein cannot be specified by sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-sequence descriptors are acceptable only with justification and clear functional/physicochemical characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monoclonal antibody claim description — sequence, antigen, or hybridoma
rubrics_metrics.description: A monoclonal antibody should, in principle, be described by specifying the amino-acid sequence in the variable regions of the heavy and light chains or the nucleic-acid sequence encoding them, by specifying the antigen recognized, or by specifying a hybridoma which produces the antibody. Specifying an antigen may be recognized as specifying the antibody if the antigen is novel and involves an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence-defined antibodies preferred; antigen-based definition permitted in limited cases when antigen novelty/inventiveness justifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant-variety claims filed before Sept 30, 2006 — asexual reproduction requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications relating to plant invention filed before September 30, 2006, a plant variety capable of asexual reproduction is the only patentable subject matter among plant varieties, and it is required to describe the method of asexual reproduction in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal/legal cutoff: earlier-filed plant applications have specific claim/form requirements under prior law (Article 31 of Old Patent Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention in biotechnology — depends on shared technical feature and contribution over prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether unity of invention is fulfilled depends on the degree of disclosure of prior arts and whether claimed items share a same or corresponding special technical feature that makes a contribution over prior art. Examples show lack of unity when claims share only origin or unrelated functions, and unity when claims share a common structural/functional motif not known in prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine common technical features and whether they materially contribute over prior art (examples 1–5 illustrate application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (industrial applicability) for biotech inventions — concrete examples of lack of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: If no specific, substantial and credible utility is asserted or inferred in the specification for genes, DNA fragments, antisense, vectors, proteins, monoclonal antibodies, microorganisms, animals, plants, etc., the invention is not industrially applicable. Examples of lack of utility include: DNA fragment described only as a probe for obtaining full-length DNA; SNPs merely described without experimental demonstration of diagnostic utility; full-length cDNA deduced solely by homology searches; protein described only by sequence without properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility must be experimentally supported or clearly explained; mere sequence information without demonstrated or credible use fails Article 29(1) requirements (case law cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpatentable inventions on public-order/morality grounds (biotech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions that inevitably contravene public order or morality are unpatentable, e.g., inventions that inevitably damage human beings or undermine human dignity (processes for cloning human beings, germ-line genetic modification, and resulting products). Also, inventions relating to transgenic animals without excluding human beings are unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-order/morality exclusions are applied where carrying out the invention would inevitably cause the stated harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmacological-effect disclosure requirement (pharmaceutical inventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pharmacological effect of a medicinal-use invention should be described in the original specification to support its medical use. Principally, pharmacological effect should be supported by clinical tests; animal or in-vitro tests can substitute clinical tests in some inventions. Specification should disclose test results or describe in great detail how the substance shows effect unless the mechanism was clearly known before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pharmacological data or detailed mechanism description is required to support medicinal-use claims; selection inventions must state effects clearly for skilled persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical specification — dose, administration, dosage form, and toxicity testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Principally, effective dose and method of administration should be described in the original specification of a medicinal-use invention; dosage form should be stated so a skilled person can carry out the invention. Acute toxicity test results may be requested during examination if toxicity is specifically doubted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical details for therapeutic use (dose, administration, dosage form) are essential for enablement and may be scrutinized for safety concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosmetics — objective evidence for claimed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of cosmetics should be confirmed by objective documents such as sensory panel test results; functional cosmetics with biochemical or physical effects require objective documentation and detailed description to prove functional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensory tests, biochemical/physical measurements, and other objective evidence expected for cosmetics/function claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims drafting for medicinal use — product recitation and specific pharmacological effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A medicinal-use invention should be recited as a product invention. Comprehensive descriptions like 'medicine' or 'therapeutic agent' are not allowable; the medicinal use should be stated as a pharmacological effect such as diagnosis, therapy, improvement (relief), treatment or prevention. Specification by pharmacological mechanism is allowed if a skilled person recognizes the mechanism as a specific pharmacological effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must specify the therapeutic effect or disease target rather than generic terms; mechanism-based claim language allowed only when it unambiguously indicates a specific medicinal use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of pharmaceutical/mode-of-use inventions — same substance with different use and mechanism consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A medicinal-use invention using the same substance can be novel if it has a different use; however, if the pharmacological effect appears to be based on the same or similar action mechanism as a cited reference, they are considered the same and lack novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed use is materially distinct or merely a rephrasing of a known mechanism/use; technical equivalence can destroy novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of differently-stated but identical inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two inventions stated differently in claims but having the same purpose and effect are deemed identical (examples: device for manufacturing medicines vs. simple processes for manufacturing; medicine vs. directions for medicine; mixture vs. process for manufacturing mixture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance and purpose/effect, not claim wording alone, determine novelty equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of process/manufacturing changes and added known processes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject of a manufacturing invention is stated differently but is based on the same pharmacological effect, it is considered identical lacking novelty. Adding a newly added process can confer novelty, but adding a publicly known or commonly used process that is not newly created does not confer novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only genuinely new process steps can give novelty; mere combination with well-known steps may fail to be novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of optical isomer inventions when racemate is disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a racemate is disclosed in the prior art, if each optical isomer not disclosed literally is reasonably recognized by a skilled person from the specification and technical knowledge at filing, the isomers may be considered publicly disclosed and thus lack novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of racemates can anticipate individual isomers if routine derivation is expected by skilled persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for medicinal-use inventions — criteria and dosage-regimen consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A medicinal invention is deemed to have inventive step if the medicinal effect is so creative and effective that it could not have been arrived at from the chemical structure of the active compound or identified by the action mechanism in cited references by a skilled person. Inventive step evaluation may consider dosage regimen or dose as elements; inventive step may be acknowledged only for specific dosage regimens/doses that provide prominent or unexpected effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dosage/regimen can contribute to inventive step only when the effect is unpredictable and significant compared to prior art; examples illustrate refusals and acceptances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for polymorphic crystal forms (pharmaceutical compounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: For polymorphic crystal-form inventions, inventive step is acknowledged if the crystal form has a different effect qualitatively or quantitatively from the compound in the cited document. The effect should be stated in the description of the crystal-form invention; if there is doubt, the effect should be proved by submitting comparative-study documents post-filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative effect data or clear description of differing effects is required to support inventive-step assertions for crystal forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-health exclusion under Article 32 — inventions threatening public health
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions that can definitely threaten public health are unpatentable under Article 32 (examples: use of harmful amounts of materials in medicines or cosmetics that exceed permissible levels). However, inventions harmful or not depending on practice may still be patentable (e.g., a medicine contraindicated for pregnant women but otherwise useful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess harmfulness relative to intended effect and permissible use; contextual regulatory status (e.g., approval under Pharmaceutical Affairs Act) affects evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of legal/technical evidence and case law in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination guidance repeatedly references judicial verdicts and the need for documentary proof (test results, investment/loan/contract records, comparative studies) to support assertions (utility, unexpected effect, practicing/preparation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner decisions rely on documented evidence and cited case law; applicants should supply supporting data where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of applicability — chapter delineation
rubrics_metrics.description: This chapter applies to inventions relating to genetic engineering and biological materials (genes, DNA fragments, vectors, proteins, antibodies, microorganisms, animals, plants) and to pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and food-related inventions as indicated in chapter headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chapter-specific criteria when examining or drafting applications in these technology areas; later chapters provide additional sector-specific rules (e.g., food).
